principles.text: Spend about 10x more time replying to other people than posting your own tweets, especially while your audience is tiny.
Don't try to fix a distribution problem by building more features. The missing piece is marketing.
Start from business fundamentals: demand, willingness to pay and acquisition cost, not a cool idea and hard work.
Write the landing page before the product, then build the product to deliver that promise.
Followers are a consequence of success. You still need a real problem, a great product and a durable channel.

sampleQA.question: How do I grow on X from zero followers?

answer.text: Spend your time connecting, not tweeting: reply to people at your level in your niche for about 30 minutes a day. That usually gets you to 500-1,000 followers.
Interact about 10x more than you post. When someone replies to or likes your reply, you show up in their feed for the next 24-72 hours.
Post from your own face and name, and turn events into problem-solution stories instead of guru one-liners.
Returns drop past a few thousand to 10K followers. At that point fix the product and build channels like SEO or affiliates.

sampleQA.question: Sales are flat. Should I build more features or do marketing?

answer.text: Marketing. In 2021 Logology spent 5 months on product and made $2,250, then 7 months on marketing and made $17,500.
2.5 years of building without marketing brought 50 sales; 6 months of only marketing brought 300.
Six months of UX work didn't lift conversion; being seen everywhere raised it 50% because people trusted them more.
Keep saying no to features until marketing carries survival.

sampleQA.question: How do I pick what to build next?

answer.text: Check the boring fundamentals first: is there demand, will customers pay enough, can you acquire them at a good cost.
Find an underserved market through search demand and G2 or Capterra reviews, then build an alternative with a clear differentiator.
Look past indie-maker niches. Old industries have less competition and can pay far more than $9/month SaaS.
Favor recurring revenue. Without it, Logology had to find 100+ new customers every month.
